title: Travel Insurance: What It Actually Covers and the Fine Print That Bites
metaDescription: Medical cover, cancellation, adventure sports exclusions, pre-existing conditions and credit card insurance — how to read a travel policy before you need it.
excerpt: Most travel insurance claims are rejected for reasons written clearly in the policy. Here is what to read before you buy, not after something goes wrong.
author: Travel Editors
content:
Travel insurance is bought in about ninety seconds, usually as a tick-box at checkout, and then never read until the worst week of someone's trip. That is precisely backwards.

The good news is that the fine print is not really that fine. Four or five clauses do most of the work, and reading them takes ten minutes.

## What Is Travel Insurance Actually For?

Not lost luggage. Luggage cover is the part people talk about and the smallest part of the value.

The real purpose is **catastrophic medical cost and evacuation**. A serious illness or accident abroad can generate a bill that runs into six figures, and a medical evacuation flight — an air ambulance from a remote region to a city hospital, or home — runs from tens of thousands to well over a hundred thousand dollars.

That is the risk you are insuring. Everything else is useful padding.

## How Much Medical Cover Do You Need?

Ignore policies advertising low medical limits. As a working guide:

- **Europe** — a minimum of €30,000 is mandated for Schengen visas, but that is a legal floor, not a sensible ceiling
- **Most of the world** — look for at least $100,000 to $250,000
- **The United States** — this is the outlier. US healthcare costs mean **$500,000 to $1,000,000** is the sensible band, and cheap policies with low US limits are close to worthless

Check that **emergency medical evacuation and repatriation** is included with its own adequate limit, and that the policy covers being transported to an appropriate facility rather than just the nearest one.

![Travel Tips travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1594069758873-e79e9075eb7d?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## The Exclusions That Cause Most Rejected Claims

**Pre-existing medical conditions.** The biggest single cause. Most standard policies exclude anything you have been diagnosed with, treated for, or taken medication for in a look-back period — often 12 to 24 months. This includes conditions you consider trivial or resolved.

The fix is straightforward but requires action: **declare everything** and either pay the medical loading or buy a policy with a pre-existing conditions waiver, which usually requires purchasing within a short window of your first trip deposit. Declaring costs money. Not declaring can void the whole policy, including for something unrelated.

**Adventure and sports activities.** Standard policies exclude a long list. The usual suspects: scuba diving beyond a certain depth or without certification, motorcycle or scooter riding — especially without a valid licence for that class — skiing off-piste, trekking above a stated altitude, bungee jumping, paragliding, white-water rafting above certain grades.

The **scooter in Southeast Asia** deserves its own warning. Renting a scooter in Thailand, Vietnam, Bali or India without a motorcycle licence valid in that country voids medical cover for any resulting accident. Road injuries are among the most common serious incidents involving travellers, and this exclusion is triggered constantly.

**Alcohol and drugs.** If intoxication contributed to the incident, cover is typically excluded. Policies vary in how strictly this is applied, but it is a real and frequently used exclusion.

**Unattended belongings.** A bag stolen from a beach towel, an unlocked car, an overhead rack you were not watching — routinely excluded. Theft cover usually requires forced entry or the item being on your person.

**Government travel advisories.** If your government advises against travel to a region and you go anyway, cover is often void for that region. Check the advisory before you book, and again before you go.

**Undeclared cancellation reasons.** Cancellation cover usually lists specific covered reasons — illness, injury, death of a close relative, jury service, serious damage to your home. Changing your mind, a work conflict, or a relationship ending are generally not among them unless you bought a "cancel for any reason" upgrade, which costs substantially more and typically reimburses only a portion.

![Travel Tips travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1620563092215-0fbc6b55cfc5?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Is Your Credit Card Insurance Enough?

Sometimes, and it is worth knowing exactly what you have. Premium cards often include trip cancellation, delay, baggage and rental car cover, and some include medical.

Check three things:

1. **Activation conditions.** Most require you to have paid for the trip — often the full fare, sometimes just part — with that card.
2. **Medical limits.** Card medical cover is often low or absent. Delay and baggage cover is common; a $500,000 medical limit is not.
3. **Trip length caps.** Card policies frequently cover only the first 30 or 60 days of a trip.

For a short trip within a well-served region, card cover is often genuinely sufficient. For long trips, remote destinations, or anywhere with expensive healthcare, it usually is not.

## When Should You Buy?

**As soon as you make the first non-refundable payment.** Two reasons:

- Cancellation cover only applies to events after you buy. A policy bought after you already know about the problem covers nothing.
- Pre-existing condition waivers and "cancel for any reason" upgrades usually require purchase within 10 to 21 days of your first deposit. Miss that window and the option is gone permanently for that trip.

## What to Do When Something Goes Wrong

The process matters as much as the policy:

- **Call the emergency assistance number first**, before treatment where possible. Many policies require pre-authorisation for non-emergency care, and failing to call can reduce or void a claim.
- **Keep every document.** Receipts, medical reports, prescriptions, police reports for theft — obtained at the time, in the country, because getting them later is usually impossible.
- **File a police report within 24 hours** for any theft. Nearly all policies require it, and nearly all have a deadline.
- **Report baggage problems to the airline before leaving the airport** and get written confirmation. Airline liability comes first; insurance covers the gap.
- **Submit promptly.** Policies have claim deadlines, often 30 to 90 days.

## A Ten-Minute Pre-Purchase Check

Before you buy, search the policy document for five words: **"pre-existing"**, **"excluded"**, **"maximum"**, **"sub-limit"** and the name of any activity you plan to do. You will find the answer to almost every question that matters.

Then check the **sub-limits**. A policy advertising $250,000 of cover may cap baggage at $500 total and $100 per item, which means your laptop is effectively uninsured. Sub-limits are where the marketing headline and the actual cover diverge.

For group trips, one more thing worth doing: **share the policy details**. If one person is incapacitated, somebody else needs the policy number and the emergency line. Keeping insurance details alongside the itinerary where the whole group can reach them — **Trypinn** works well for this — costs nothing and matters exactly once, on the worst day of the trip.
